newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.N. sees growing problems for world refugees.
newsitem.headline: U.N. sees growing problems for world refugees.

text.p: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako Ogata said on Monday observance of agreed standards for protection of the 26 million refugees and displaced people around the world had declined in 1996.

In a speech to her UNHCR agency's Executive Committee, she also appealed to government leaders to fight prejudice against refugees and to agree on a more equal share among major countries of the burden of providing asylum.

During the current year, she declared, "access to territory has been either denied outright, as a result of push-offs of boat arrivals and rejections at borders, or complicated by new legislative restrictions".

"Deadly attacks on refugee camps, sexual abuse of refugee women and children, forcible conscription of refugee men and children, and abusive detention have seriously undermined safety during asylum," she declared.
Additionally, the former Japanese diplomat and academic said, "the voluntary nature of repatriation is increasingly being undermined by a mounting number of forcible returns".

She made no direct reference to any country, but among other developments known to have concerned UNHCR officials was the recent decision by German states to begin the gradual repatriation of some 320,000 Bosnian war refugees.

However, Ogata said the burden of sheltering refugees was "very unevenly divided, between and within continents," noting that Germany hosted more Bosnians than all other West European countries together.

At the same time, she added, many countries had continued to open their borders to refugees -- including Iran, which has admitted some 42,000 Kurds over the last few weeks in the wake of fighting in northern Iraq.

The world's population of "refugees" -- defined as those who have crossed national borders -- declined from 14.5 million in early 1995 to 13.2 million earlier this year, partly because there were no humanitarian emergencies on the scale of the early 1990s.

But there is a similar number of people "displaced" within their countries, who are also aided by the UNHCR in areas like former Yugoslavia and the Great Lakes region of central Africa, meaning 26.1 million people are under the U.N. agency's wing.
Africa remained the region with the highest number of refugees, followed by Asia, Europe, Latin America, and North America, Ogata said.
"While there has been important progress towards durable solutions in many parts of the globe, there remain enormous new challenges in several post-Cold War conflicts," she declared.

The High Commissioner left no doubt of her growing concern over problems posed for UNHCR operations by the nearly two million Rwandan refugees in camps inside Zaire, Tanzania and other countries in the region.
"The risk of inter-state tension is compounded when international protection is abused by people not deserving it because they are guilty of genocide or other heinous crimes," she declared.

U.N. officials say that among the refugees are many people who organised or took part in the genocide directed by the country's former Hutu-led administration in which up to a million people, mainly Tutsis, died.
"Probably never before has my Office found its humanitarian concerns in the midst of such a lethal quagmire of political and security interests," Ogata said.

"While our humanitarian assistance and protection serve an innocent, silent majority of needy and anxious refugees, they also serve the militants who have an interest in maintaining the status quo. This cannot go on," she declared.
